bibliography.abstract: Recurrent air threats turn civilian protection into a continuing condition of urban mobility. This study applies GIS-based cumulative-opportunity analysis to define the Protective Shelter Accessibility Index (PSI), a spatial screening measure of the average number of designated shelters reachable from public transport stops through the pedestrian network within 2-, 5- and 15-minute planning horizons. The index is applied to 348 transport analysis zones in Kharkiv and compares a 2019 pre-invasion baseline with a 2024 wartime-adapted operational state. Of 1,212 registered structures screened for the later state, 547 met the eligibility rules used in the network analysis, compared with 87 underground facilities in the baseline. Eligible shelter density increased from 0.25 to 1.56 shelters km⁻². The share of zones with any reachable shelter rose from 28.2% to 51.1% at two minutes, from 35.3% to 54.0% at five minutes and from 45.4% to 61.2% at fifteen minutes. Nevertheless, 135 zones remained without a reachable shelter at fifteen minutes, and the median wartime-adapted zone remained below one reachable shelter per stop. Walking-speed sensitivity defines conservative and upper accessibility bounds. The findings identify critical mobility interfaces where transport, civil-protection and spatial-planning interventions should be coordinated. The analytical sequence is transferable, while warning horizons, facility eligibility and governance arrangements require local validation. The stop-origin specification distinguishes initial shelter coverage from the average availability of reachable alternatives and supports coordinated appraisal of transport and protective infrastructure. Clinical trial Not applicable.

en.caveats: The empirical findings reflect specific walking-speed assumptions and local facility eligibility criteria that must be re-calibrated when transferring the methodology to other conflict zones.
en.what: The study introduces the Protective Shelter Accessibility Index (PSI), a GIS-based cumulative-opportunity metric measuring pedestrian access to emergency shelters from public transit stops across 2-, 5-, and 15-minute walking horizons. Applied to 348 transport analysis zones in Kharkiv, Ukraine, it compares 2019 baseline conditions against a 2024 wartime configuration. Between these periods, eligible shelter density rose from 0.25 to 1.56 facilities per km², increasing the share of zones with 2-minute shelter access from 28.2% to 51.1%, though 135 zones still lacked any accessible shelter within 15 minutes.
en.why: It establishes a quantitative framework for integrating civil protection into daily transit planning, replacing static shelter counts with dynamic, walk-time-based accessibility metrics for populations navigating recurring aerial threats.
